prompt: Proposal for a study app: after each written answer, ask a model to score it out of 100, store the number, and show the learner a trend line of their scores over the past month. Critique it.

criteria: States that the same answer submitted twice can come back with different scores
Says the trend line then plots model noise rather than the learner's progress
Names the loss of trust the first time the learner notices an identical answer scored differently
Proposes checkable criteria the learner ticks off instead of a number

prompt: You feed one unchanged answer to the same grader on ten separate nights. Estimate the spread you would see in a 0-100 score, estimate it for a five-box checklist, and say which boxes would be the unstable ones.

criteria: Gives a numeric range for the score that spans at least ten points
Gives a smaller spread for the checklist, such as one box flipping between nights
Says the unstable boxes are the ones whose wording leaves room for interpretation
Explains that a box asks whether one specific claim is present, which is a narrower judgment than a number

prompt: Which of these rubric lines can a learner check against their own written answer in two seconds?

options: Shows a firm grasp of the tradeoffs involved
Explains the idea at the right level for the audience
Says the retry is safe only because the write is idempotent
Covers the important points about idempotency

prompt: True or false: asking the model for three independent scores of the same answer and averaging them removes the instability that makes a 0-100 grade untrustworthy.

criteria: States that averaging narrows the spread without removing it
Says the three samples share the same bias, so they are not independent the way averaging assumes
Names the cost of three calls for a number that still drifts between nights
Points out that a checkable criterion sidesteps the problem rather than shrinking it
States that averaging narrows the spread without removing it
Says the three samples share the same bias, so they are not independent the way averaging assumes
Names the cost of three calls for a number that still drifts between nights
Points out that a checkable criterion sidesteps the problem rather than shrinking it

prompt: You read a model's walkthrough of a tricky query plan, follow every step, and close the tab satisfied. The next day you cannot reconstruct the argument. Explain what actually happened.

criteria: Names recognition and production as two separate abilities
States that following an argument leans on the text as a crutch
Says retrieval from a blank page is the step that was skipped
Gives a way to test the difference before closing the tab

prompt: You have two free hours the day before a technical conversation about a topic you half know. Which use of them leaves you most able to talk about it?

options: Re-reading your notes twice, annotating every part you are unsure about
Working through a worked example line by line, checking each step against the docs
Writing an explanation from memory, then checking it and closing the gaps
Watching a recorded talk at half speed, pausing to take structured notes

prompt: Put these steps in the order that turns a page you have read into something you can say out loud.

items: Compare your version against the source and mark what you missed
Read the explanation once, then close it
Come back later and drill only the parts you missed
Write the explanation from a blank page without looking

prompt: A teammate says deliberate practice on fundamentals is a waste of time now, because anything can be looked up in seconds. Give them your honest counter.

criteria: Concedes that lookup is fine for facts you can look up
Names a moment where lookup is unavailable, such as a live conversation
States that fluency comes from retrieval, not from access
Stops short of claiming memorisation beats understanding

prompt: A fact came back in front of you tonight for the first time in four days, and you produced the answer without hesitating. How far out should it go before you see it again? Give a range and show the reasoning that gets you there.

criteria: Gives a range instead of a single unsupported number
Pushes the next gap out past the four days just survived
Ties the size of the jump to how little effort the recall took
Names a wrong or hesitant answer as what would collapse the interval back down

prompt: You reread a chapter three times on Sunday and do badly on a Wednesday quiz. A friend read it once, then on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday tried to write down what it said before opening it. They do well. Explain what their study did that yours did not.

criteria: Names pulling the answer out of memory as the act that strengthens it
States that rereading builds familiarity with the page, not access to the fact
Says the gaps between attempts are what make the recall effortful
Notes that the fluent feeling during rereading is why the failure is a surprise

prompt: Two people study the same twenty facts for the same total number of minutes. One does every minute in a single sitting; the other splits the minutes across five days. Both are tested a month later. What happens?

options: The one who spread the minutes across five days remembers more
They come out about even, because the total study time was the same
The single-sitting one remembers more, having had less time in between to forget
The spread-out one wins on a test taken right after studying, but the gap closes by a month

prompt: Put these four moments of a single review of one fact into the order that leaves the strongest memory behind.

items: Check what you wrote against the answer key and mark it
Read the question and close the notes
Write down the best answer you can produce from memory
Schedule the next sighting further out than the gap you just came through

prompt: A study app keeps every answer a person has ever given in a single localStorage key, rewriting the whole array after each question. The most dedicated user has been at it nightly for two years. What breaks first?

criteria: Names the roughly 5MB per-origin quota as the ceiling being approached
States that the write throws once the quota is exceeded rather than failing quietly
Says the rewrite is synchronous, so it blocks the main thread as the array grows
Proposes trimming the history or keeping it out of the per-question write path

prompt: A page runs `localStorage.setItem('count', 3)`. On the next load it runs `const n = localStorage.getItem('count');` then `console.log(n + 1);`. What appears in the console?

answer.explain: Everything comes back out of localStorage as a string, so `getItem` returns `"3"` and `+` concatenates instead of adding. Numbers have to be converted on the way out with `Number(...)` or `parseInt(...)`, for the same reason objects have to be JSON round-tripped.

prompt: This helper is supposed to persist a progress object. It never throws and never logs, yet the value read back on the next load is useless. Which line is the problem?

answer.why: localStorage holds strings and nothing else, so handing `setItem` an object stores the result of its `toString` — the literal text `[object Object]` — with no error raised anywhere. Serialise on the way in with `JSON.stringify(progress)` and parse on the way out.

prompt: Match each detail of a four-question review session to the person it exists for.

left: A hard ceiling of four questions
Filled and unfilled pips along the top of the screen
A screen that comes up after the last answer and says the session is over
right: Someone part-way through who wants to know how much is left
Someone weighing up whether to open the app at all tonight
Someone who has just answered the last question and does not realise it

prompt: True or false: the screen shown after the last question is a nicety, since a person can already tell they are finished when no further question arrives.

criteria: States that nothing appearing is indistinguishable from the app having stalled
Says the end screen marks the session as completed rather than abandoned
Names the explicit stop as what gives permission to put the device down
Notes that without it the natural next move is to go looking for more

prompt: Someone trying your review app asks why it refuses to give them a fifth question when they were enjoying themselves and had time to spare. Answer them.

criteria: States that the ceiling is set for the worst night, not the best one
Says an open-ended session makes the decision to start a larger one
Points out that the end is visible before the first question is answered
Admits the cost to the motivated evening and says why the trade is taken anyway

prompt: Name a kind of studying where a hard four-question ceiling would be the wrong design, and say what you would bound instead.

criteria: Names a case such as cramming to a deadline or clearing a first-time backlog
Says what replaces the fixed count, such as a time box or a due queue
Keeps some end point in view rather than removing the bound altogether
States the signal that would send you back to the fixed count

prompt: An app greets you with '148 cards due' so that you always know where you stand. Critique that number.

criteria: Says the figure only ever grows during an absence and reads as debt
States that a large count makes a four-question session feel futile
Notes that the number measures the gap, not anything tonight can change
Proposes showing the small fixed session instead of the backlog

prompt: Two apps hold identical content. One keeps a daily streak; the other records nothing about attendance. A user of each misses eleven days in a row. What does the streak most reliably change about day twelve?

options: It attaches a cost to returning that the other app does not have
It makes returning likelier, because the user has already invested in the streak
Nothing, since the questions waiting on day twelve are the same either way
It shortens the session the returning user is handed

prompt: Someone opens a review app for the first time in three weeks. Which of these, if the app puts them on screen, make it likelier that the person closes it without answering anything? Select all that apply.

options: A banner announcing that their 41-day streak has ended
A count of 300 items now overdue
The first question, already on screen and ready to answer
A calendar grid with three weeks of blank squares
A session that is the same four questions long as it was three weeks ago

prompt: A colleague wants a streak counter plus a 'your 40-day streak has ended' banner, arguing that streaks are the best-evidenced retention feature in consumer apps. Push back.

criteria: States that the banner fires at the exact moment someone chose to come back
Says a broken streak reframes a return as a failure rather than a win
Separates nightly compliance from what the app is actually for
Lands on a recommendation instead of laying out both sides

prompt: The app opens straight onto a question. One user wants to skip tonight's subject, a second wants to drill one specific area before a morning meeting, and a third wants to see how many questions they have answered in total. What breaks first?

criteria: Names the drill-one-area request as the one with no path at all
States that the design is tuned for the ordinary nightly case, not these three
Says restoring a picker puts the decision back in front of everyone
Proposes serving the edge case somewhere off the opening path

prompt: An opening screen that asks 'which deck?' and 'how long tonight?' puts two ______ in front of someone whose willingness is nearly gone, and each one is a place where the app gets closed instead.
Opening the app lands you directly on a question — no home screen, no deck picker, no start button. Walk through what that removal buys, and name what it costs.

criteria: States that every choice before the first question is a place to drop out
Says the design makes the decision in advance so a tired person does not have to
Names a concrete thing now impossible, such as picking tonight's topic
Notes that the cost falls on the rarer user who wanted the control

prompt: Someone taps the icon of a review app that has no home screen and no start button. Put these four moments in the order they happen, from the tap to the second question.

items: The answer is graded against its rubric
The next question replaces the last one
A question is on screen with the input already focused

prompt: You ship a browser-only app that calls a paid model API with the key written into the JavaScript, and you lock the key to your own domain in the provider's console. What breaks first, and what did that domain restriction actually buy you?

criteria: Says the key is readable in the page source or the network tab
States that the origin or referrer header is sent by the client and can be forged
Names quota exhaustion or an unexpected bill as the first visible symptom
Concludes that only a server you control can hold the key

prompt: A page served as static files needs to call a paid API. Four arrangements are proposed. Which one actually keeps the key out of the visitor's reach?

options: Fetch the key from a `config.json` sitting beside the page at startup
Inject the key at build time from an environment variable
Send the request to a server you control, which attaches the key and forwards it
Write the key into `localStorage` on first load and read it from there afterwards

prompt: True or false: running the bundle through a minifier so the API key is not greppable in the shipped source makes it acceptable to keep the key in the browser. Justify the verdict.

criteria: States that the running code must hand the real key to the network layer
Notes the key then appears in plain text in the request headers
Says obfuscation raises the effort without moving the trust boundary
Points at the devtools network tab as where it surfaces anyway

prompt: A product owner with no engineering background asks why you need to run and pay for a small server just to call a paid API, when the thing you built is only a web page. Answer them.

criteria: States that anything the browser downloads can be read by the person using it
Avoids jargon such as CORS, bundler or environment variable
Names the concrete risk: a stranger spending against your account
Ends on one recommendation rather than a menu of options

prompt: A list of fifty buttons is thrown away and rebuilt from scratch whenever the data changes, yet one click handler attached once to the surrounding container keeps working on the new buttons. Explain the mechanism.

criteria: States that a click travels up from the clicked node through its ancestors
Says the handler inspects `event.target` to learn which button was hit
Explains that freshly created children need no listener of their own
Notes that the container element itself is never replaced

prompt: An outer `div` and an inner `button` each get a click listener that logs its own name. Both are registered with the default options and neither calls `stopPropagation`. Someone clicks the button. What gets logged, in what order?

answer.explain: Listeners registered without `capture` run in the bubble phase, so the innermost target fires first and the event then travels up: `button`, then `div`.

prompt: This delegated click handler never selects anything, whatever row the user clicks. Find the line at fault.

answer.why: The click lands on the inner `<span>`, so `e.target` is that span, not the `<li>` carrying `data-id`. The handler has to walk up first: `e.target.closest('.row').dataset.id`.

prompt: One delegated listener on a container is usually the move. When is a listener per element the better choice instead?

criteria: Names an event that does not bubble, such as focus or scroll
Says the delegated handler must filter targets, which breaks as markup shifts
Gives a case where a child calls `stopPropagation` and the container never hears it
Mentions a small fixed set of elements as a reason not to bother

prompt: A page loads its data at startup with `const data = await fetch(url).then(r => r.json())` and renders from it. Months later the file is moved and the host answers that path with its own 404 page. What breaks first, and what does the visitor see?

criteria: States that `fetch` does not reject on a 404 response
Says `r.json()` is the thing that fails, because it is handed HTML
Names an empty screen as what the visitor actually gets
Proposes checking `r.ok` before parsing the body

prompt: Review this startup path: the page fetches three separate JSON files, awaiting each one before requesting the next, with the whole block in a single `try` that logs to the console if anything throws. What would you change?

criteria: Says the three requests are independent and should overlap
Names `Promise.all` or starting all three before awaiting as the fix
Points out that a console log leaves nothing on screen for the visitor
Says one shared `try` cannot say which of the three failed

prompt: Put these steps into the order a careful on-demand JSON load performs them.

items: Swap the loading state for the rendered content
Check `response.ok` and throw with the status when it is false
Put a visible loading state on screen and call `fetch`

prompt: The network tab shows the file arriving with a 200, but the screen stays empty. One line explains it.

answer.why: `loadBank` is `async`, so it hands back a Promise, not the parsed body. `bank.questions` is `undefined` and the render draws nothing — the call needs `await loadBank('data')` inside an async caller, or a `.then`.

prompt: A static host answers each request by handing back a file from disk unchanged, running none of your ______ in the process — which is why a request for a path that does not exist comes back as a bare ______ instead of hitting a route handler.
Your site is a few hundred kilobytes of HTML, CSS, JS and JSON on a static host behind a CDN, and it takes ten thousand visits a month. Estimate the monthly bill, and say what the number is made of.

criteria: Lands at or very near zero dollars a month
Multiplies page weight by visits to get a few gigabytes of transfer
Says bandwidth and stored bytes are the only meters running
Notes there is no per-request compute charge to pay at all

prompt: Which of these hold for a site served by a static file host?

options: Every visitor requesting a given path receives identical bytes
Any value the page needs at run time is readable by the visitor
The host can check who is asking before it hands over a file, with nothing else added
Absorbing a traffic spike is mostly the CDN's problem rather than yours
The host can tailor the page per signed-in user before sending it
Something one visitor types can be kept for the next visitor without another service

prompt: A teammate wants to add a quick server-side password check to an app that lives on a static file host, saying it is only a few lines. Push back on the proposal.

criteria: States that the host runs none of your code per request
Says any check written into the page executes on the visitor's own machine
Names a concrete route such as a serverless function or a hosted auth service
Acknowledges the outcome the teammate is trying to reach
